Audience

  • This white paper is intended for sales engineers, field consultants, IT administrators, customers, and anyone else who is interested in configuring and deploying RHOCP and PowerStore CSI with Dell PowerStore as the underlying software-defined infrastructure.

    Readers are expected to have an understanding and working knowledge of containers, Kubernetes, RHOCP, Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS), replication capabilities, PostgreSQLdatabases, and PowerStore systems.

Conclusion

  • This paper demonstrates how Dell’s CSM for Replication, combined with Dell PowerStore and RHOCP provide a robust and enterprise‑grade foundation for protecting stateful, cloud‑native workloads across distributed environments. By extending Kubernetes with native replication intelligence, the solution ensures that the PVs and associated metadata remain synchronized across clusters, enabling seamless failover, reprotection, and recovery workflows.

    Through PowerStore’s asynchronous and synchronous replication capabilities, organizations gain zero or low RPO/RTO outcomes, automated cross‑cluster data protection, and simplified disaster recovery operations. The integration of DellCSIReplicationGroup resources and multi‑cluster controllers further enhances operational consistency, ensuring that storage policies and replicated volumes remain aligned with OpenShift’s declarative management model. PowerStore Metro and file replication add protection for active‑active and file‑based workloads, improving flexibility and availability.

    Together, these technologies deliver a comprehensive and scalable DR framework that supports business continuity, minimizes downtime, and safeguards mission‑critical applications across hybrid and multicloud environments. This unified approach empowers enterprises to confidently run, protect, and recover virtualized and containerized workloads with resilience and operational efficiency.

Dell CSM Operator deployment

  • Install CSM operator

    Follow the steps below to install CSM Operator.

    1. Log in to the RHOCP web console at https://<your-cluster-url>:8443 using an account with cluster-admin privileges.

      Open OperatorHub by selecting Operators > OperatorHub in the left-hand menu.

    2. Search for “Dell Container Storage Modules” in the search bar and locate the CSM Operator in the results.
    3. Click the Dell Container Storage Modules (Certified) card, review the details, and click Install.
    4. Configure the installation by leaving the Update channel as stable, selecting All namespaces on the cluster for Installation mode, confirming openshift-operators as the Installed Namespace, and choosing Automatic for the approval strategy. Then click Install.
    5. Monitor the installation status as it progresses from Installing to Succeeded. Confirm that the operator is displaying as “ready for use.”
    6. Select Operators > Installed Operators to verify that the operator is displayed in the list.

Dell PowerStore

  • Dell PowerStore overview

    The PowerStore platform is a unified storage array that can service block and file resources along with numerous data services and efficiencies. PowerStore is ideal for traditional and modern workloads, including relational databases, electronic medical record applications, and content repositories, among many others.

    PowerStore has two purpose-built platforms:

    • The 2U, two-node dual-socket Intel® Xeon® platform, which is used for the PowerStore 1200, 3200, 5200, and 9200 models.
    • The 2U, two-node single-socket Intel® Xeon® platform, is used for the PowerStore 500 model.

    These platforms run the exact same version of software and can be clustered and managed together coherently. For more information about PowerStore platforms, see Dell PowerStore: Introduction to the Platform.

    Organizations that use new applications and solutions require dependable storage and often face the challenge of doing more with less. PowerStore addresses this challenge by packaging a powerful storage system into a cost-efficient and space-efficient profile. PowerStore features and benefits include:

    • Active/active architecture
    • Multiple protocol support, including iSCSI, Fibre Channel, NVMe/FC, NVMe/TCP, SMB, FTP, SFTP, and NFS
    • Unified offering serving block and file storage
    • Simplified, modern user interface
    • Inline data reduction
    • Local and remote native data protection

    PowerStore achieves new levels of operational simplicity and agility. It uses container- based microservices architecture, advanced storage technologies, and integrated machine learning to unlock the power of your data. It offers predictive analytics to easily monitor, analyze, and troubleshoot the environment. PowerStore is highly adaptable, providing the flexibility to host specialized workloads, and fits seamlessly into existing infrastructures to meet industry requirements. No matter where your business strategy takes you, PowerStore’s full-featured, adaptable design can help you build your unique breakthrough.

Dell PowerStore

  • Dell PowerStore CSI/CSM

    An important component outside PowerStore that enables a flexible consumption model for Kubernetes is the PowerStore CSI driver, developed as a part of the Dell Kubernetes strategy. Once the CSI driver for PowerStore is installed in a Kubernetes based cluster, it can be used to provision persistent volumes from the underlying PowerStore storage system.

    The CSI driver is a storage broker that dynamically provisions volumes from PowerStore through its API to the Kubernetes cluster. Once the volume is available on PowerStore, it is immediately mapped to the requesting pod. If a pod is destroyed or rescheduled, the CSI plug-in ensures that the volumes are remapped upon rescheduling of that pod.

    Dell CSM for PowerStore extends the standard CSI capabilities with additional key values, where each module is responsible for a different benefit. These modules help achieve:

    Observability
    Provide visibility into storage performance and capacity through integration with tools such as Prometheus and Grafana, allowing administrators to monitor metrics such as bandwidth, IOPS, and response times.
    Replication
    Enable replication and disaster recovery capabilities, allowing for the replication of volume groups and facilitating application restart in case of planned or unplanned migrations.
    Resiliency
    Enhance the resilience of Kubernetes applications by detecting node failures, control plane network failures, and storage array I/O failures, and taking necessary actions to maintain application availability.
    Authorization
    Provides storage and Kubernetes administrators the ability to apply RBAC for Dell CSI Drivers. It does this by deploying a proxy between the CSI driver and the storage system to enforce role-based access and usage rules.

    These modules currently include observability, replication, resiliency, and authorization. For more information, see Dell CSM documentation.

Deploy PostgreSQL Application

  • Deploy PostgreSQL

    To deploy PostgreSQL, follow these steps:

    1. Download and install the PostgreSQL software on the VM: 
      #sudo dnf install -y https://download.postgresql.org/pub/repos/yum/reporpms/EL-9-x86_64/pgdg-redhat-repo-latest.noarch.rpm
      #sudo dnf -qy module disable postgresql
      #sudo dnf install -y postgresql16-server
    2. Prior to initializing the PostgreSQL database, set up directories and ownership: 
      #sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vdb
      #sudo mkfs.xfs /dev/vdc
      #sudo mkdir /mnt/data
      #sudo mkdir /mnt/logs
      #sudo mount /dev/vdb /mnt/data/
      #sudo mount /dev/vdc /mnt/logs/
      #sudo chown postgres:postgres /mnt/data/
      #sudo chown postgres:postgres /mnt/logs/
      #sudo chmod 0700 /mnt/data/
      #sudo chmod 0700 /mnt/logs
      #su – postgres
    3. Install Postgres: 
      #/usr/pgsql-16/bin/initdb -D /mnt/data/
    4. Start Postgres: 
      #/usr/pgsql-16/bin/pg_ctl -D /mnt/data/ -l /mnt/logs/db1.logfile -o "-p 5432" start
      The PostgreSQL database server software processes are successfully initialized, running, and listening for the client connectivity at the configured port.
    5. Create the user databases with your preferred database name and verify that the database is created. 
      #sudo -u postgres createdb -h localhost -p 5432 mydb1
      #su - postgres
      #psql -p 5432 -d mydb1 -U postgres
      psql (16.6)
      Type "help" for help.
      mydb1=#
      A new PostgreSQL database mydb1 has been created successfully, and the postgres user can log in to it.
    6. Run the following command to generate workloads on the PostgreSQL database using the pgbench. 
      # pgbench -U postgres -i -s 8000 mydb1
      creating tables...
      generating data (client-side)...
      800000000 of 800000000 tuples (100%) done (elapsed 873.29 s, remaining 0.00 s)
      For more information about running workloads using pgbench, see PostgreSQL documentation.

Deploy PowerStore CSI Driver

  • Prepare PowerStore CSI

    Define a configuration file (config.yaml) to support replication across two clusters. Include both source and target storage system endpoints, globalID, credentials and block protocol type as iSCSI. Store this configuration securely as a Kubernetes secret in the PowerStore namespace using oc create secret generic and apply it using oc apply -f.

    # Create a dedicated OpenShift project for PowerStore CSI resources
    oc new-project powerstore

    # Sample output
    Now using project "powerstore" on server "https://api.<cluster-url>:6443".

    # Create PowerStore CSI configuration file for replication support
    # config.yaml includes both source and target array endpoints, credentials and iSCSI protocol
    cat <<EOF > config.yaml
    arrays:
    - endpoint: "https://<source-array-ip>/api/rest"
      globalID: "<source-array-id>"
      username: "<username>"
      password: "<password>"
      skipCertificateValidation: true
      blockProtocol: "ISCSI"
    - endpoint: "https://<target-array-ip>/api/rest"
      globalID: "<target-array-id>"
      username: "<username>"
      password: "<password>"
      skipCertificateValidation: true
      blockProtocol: "ISCSI"
    EOF

    # Create a Kubernetes secret from the config.yaml file
    oc create secret generic powerstore-config --from-file=config=config.yaml -n powerstore --dry-run=client -o yaml > secret-powerstore-config.yaml

    # Apply the secret
    oc apply -f secret-powerstore-config.yaml

    # Verify secret creation
    oc get secret -n powerstore

    # Sample output
    NAME                TYPE     DATA   AGE
    powerstore-config   Opaque   1      <age>

Deploy PowerStore CSI Driver

  • Preconfigure the CSM Replication

    The Container Storage Modules Operator installs the Replication module for supported Dell CSI Drivers, deploying the Replication sidecar and controller Manager. To configure Replication prior to installation using Container Storage Modules Operator, you need:

    • A source cluster, which is the main cluster.
    • A target cluster, which will serve as the disaster recovery cluster.

    The csm-replication GitHub repository is cloned to your source cluster as part of the installation. On your source cluster, run the following to clone and build the repctl tool:

    #git clone -b v1.13.0 https://github.com/dell/csm-replication.git
    #cd csm-replication/repctl
    #make build

    Alternatively, you can download a prebuilt repctl binary from the Releases page.

    #wget https://github.com/dell/csm-replication/releases/download/v1.13.0/repctl-linux-amd64
    #mv repctl-linux-amd64 repctl
    #chmod +x repctl

    The rest of the instructions assume that your current working directory is the csm-replication/repctl directory.

    To configure Replication, perform the following steps:

    1. Collect the cluster admin configurations for each of the clusters.
      In the following example the source cluster, ocp-1 uses configuration /root/.kube/kubeconfig-rk-ps-ocp01 and the target cluster, ocp-2 uses the configuration /root/.config/kubeconfig-ocp-cluster. Use repctl to add the clusters: 
      #./repctl cluster add -f "/root/.kube/kubeconfig-rk-ps-ocp01","/root/.kube/kubeconfig-ocp-cluster" -n "ocp-1","ocp-2"
      INFO Adding clusters
      INFO ocp-1
      INFO Successfully created ocp-1 in /root/.repctl/clusters folder. 25040 bytes copied
      INFO ocp-2
      INFO Successfully created ocp-2 in /root/.repctl/clusters folder. 12158 bytes copied
    2. Inject the service account’s configuration into the clusters. 
      #./repctl cluster inject --custom-configs "/root/.repctl/clusters/ocp-1"
      #./repctl cluster inject --custom-configs "/root/.repctl/clusters/ocp-2"
    3. Customize the examples/powerstore_example_values.yaml sample config. Set the values for sourceClusterID and targetClusterID to the same names used in step 1.
    4. Create the replication storage class using the modified configuration from step 3: 
      #./repctl create sc --from-config ./examples/powerstore_example_values.yaml
    5. Verify replication storage classes at source and target: 
      [root@ocp-csah repctl]# oc get sc
      NAME                     PROVISIONER                  RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE   ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE
      powerstore-replication   csi-powerstore.dellemc.com   Retain          Immediate           false                  88s
    6. Install the PowerStore CSI driver on the source cluster according to the instructions for Install CSI driver using CSM Operator. Repeat the installation of the CSI driver on the target cluster. Ensure that replication is enabled in the custom resource YAML used for installation, under the components field.
      Note: As of CSM release 1.14, all Custom Resource Definitions that are required for Replication functionality are installed by the CSM Operator automatically when a Replication-enabled driver is installed.

Deploy PowerStore CSI Driver

  • Install CSI driver using CSM Operator

    CSM Custom Resource (CR) is a Kubernetes‑native configuration object used by the Dell CSM Operator to deploy and manage the CSI driver for PowerStore and optional enterprise‑grade CSM add‑on modules.

    1. Create a Custom Resource ContainerStorageModule for PowerStore with replication set to enabled under the components field.
    2. Deploy the PowerStore CSI driver using the ContainerStorageModule custom resource. 
      #oc create -f csm-powerstore.yaml
      containerstoragemodule.storage.dell.com/powerstore created
    3. Verify the CR and CSI driver deployment. 
      #oc get csm powerstore -n powerstore
      NAME         CREATIONTIME   CSIDRIVERTYPE   CONFIGVERSION   STATE
      powerstore   103m           powerstore      v2.15.1         Succeeded

Deploy PowerStore CSI Driver

  • Configure a replication StorageClass

    Define a StorageClass YAML file (sc-powerstore.yaml) to provision Persistent Volumes with replication enabled between source and target clusters. This includes parameters like volume binding mode, provisioner, and reclaim policy, replication mode, remote storage class name, remote cluster ID, remote system, RPO value and the source array details used for volume creation.

    Apply the StorageClass using oc apply -f and confirm creation using oc get storageclass.

    [root@ocp-csah]#cat sc-powerstore.yaml
     
    apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
    kind: StorageClass
    metadata:
      name: "sc-powerstore"
    provisioner: "csi-powerstore.dellemc.com"
    reclaimPolicy: Delete
    allowVolumeExpansion: true
    volumeBindingMode: Immediate
    parameters:
      replication.storage.dell.com/isReplicationEnabled: "true"
      replication.storage.dell.com/mode: "ASYNC"
      replication.storage.dell.com/remoteStorageClassName: "powerstore-replication"
      replication.storage.dell.com/remoteClusterID: "PSc6a9a71e78ca"
      replication.storage.dell.com/remoteSystem: "PowerStore-Cluster"
      replication.storage.dell.com/rpo: Zero
      replication.storage.dell.com/ignoreNamespaces: "false"
     
    "
      arrayID: "PS8a9e82dd3e03"
      csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: "xfs"

    # Apply the StorageClass
    oc apply -f sc-powerstore.yaml

    # Confirm the StorageClass is created
    oc get storageclass

    # Sample expected output
    NAME                     PROVISIONER                  RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE   ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE
    powerstore-replication   csi-powerstore.dellemc.com   Retain          Immediate           false                  58m
    sc-powerstore            csi-powerstore.dellemc.com   Delete          Immediate           true                   2m39s

Failover Test from the PowerStore UI

  • Test procedure

    Follow the steps below to perform this operation:

    1. Select a replication session in the PowerStore UI.
    2. Click Start Failover Test.
    3. PowerStore activates the destination volume using the selected replication point.
    4. Applications or VMs can mount and run from this test version of the data.
    5. When testing is complete, choose one of:
      Option Description
      Stop the failover test revert to normal replication with updated data from the source
      Failover to current test data promote test data and make the destination the new source

Install RHOCP

  • Prerequisites

    Before starting the deployment, make sure the following prerequisites are fulfilled. For detailed information, see the OpenShift Assisted Installer Prerequisites documentation.

    DNS Configuration
    Ensure that DNS records for the ingress and API Virtual IP addresses (VIPs) are properly configured. These VIPs are managed by the RHOCP cluster itself, eliminating the need for an external load balancer.
    SSH Public Key
    Generate an SSH public key on the bastion node that will be used to access RHOCP cluster nodes. For guidance on generating the key pair, see Generating a Key Pair for Cluster Node SSH Access.
    NTP Server
    Set up an NTP server to ensure time synchronization among all cluster hosts, ensuring consistency across the RHOCP environment.
    Connectivity
    As part of the network requirements, ensure that all RHOCP cluster nodes have internet connectivity. Because this is a "connected" deployment, the nodes need access to external resources for the installation process.
    Note: To install RHOCP in a disconnected environment, follow the instructions in Installing a cluster in a disconnected environment.

Install RHOCP

  • RHOCP deployment steps

    To install the RHOCP cluster using the Assisted Installer:

    1. Log in to the Red Hat Console and select RHOCP.
    2. In the Cluster List, click Create cluster, choose Datacenter, and then click Create cluster under Assisted Installer.
    3. Cluster Setup
      1. Enter a Cluster name, Base domain, and OpenShift version.
      2. Select Static network configuration and click Next.
    4. Configure static networking (IPv4, VLAN ID, DNS, CIDR, gateway, NTP).
    5. In Host specific configurations, map each interface to the host’s MAC address and click Next.
    6. Add hosts using Discovery ISO.
      1. Under Host Discovery, click Add Hosts.
      2. Paste the SSH public key that you generated in Prerequisites.
      3. Click Generate Discovery ISO.
      4. Click Download Discovery ISO.
    7. Boot all hosts using the discovery ISO.
    8. Assign roles (control plane/worker) once the hosts are discovered.
    9. Configure cluster networking: Machine CIDR, API VIP, Ingress VIP, and validate DNS resolution.
    10. Review the configuration and click Install Cluster.
    11. After installation, download the kubeconfig and kubeadmin passwords.
    12. Copy the kubeconfig to the bastion node and validate: 
      # export KUBECONFIG=/root/kubeconfig-ocp-cluster
      # kubectl get nodes
      NAME                    STATUS   ROLES                         AGE     VERSION
      ocp-host-1.dell.local   Ready    control-plane,master,worker   1d   v1.31.13
      ocp-host-2.dell.local   Ready    control-plane,master,worker   1d   v1.31.13
      ocp-host-3.dell.local   Ready    control-plane,master,worker   1d   v1.31.13

Home > Storage > PowerStore > White Papers > Building Resiliency for Red Hat OpenShift with Dell PowerStore and CSM Replication > Introduction

Introduction

  • Dell’s Container Storage Modules (CSM) for Replication extends Kubernetes-native storage capabilities to deliver robust, enterprise - class disaster recovery (DR) and failover automation for applications running on Red Hat OpenShift Container Platform (RHOCP). Integrated with Dell PowerStore, the solution enables organizations to protect stateful container workloads through CSM Replication while maintaining application portability and business continuity across clusters.

    CSM Replication leverages PowerStore’s native asynchronous and synchronous replication to create and maintain replicated Persistent Volumes (PVs) and volume groups across paired RHOCP clusters. These capabilities enable rapid, predictable, and policy‑driven failover during planned maintenance or unplanned outages.

iSCSI configuration

  • iSCSI VLAN setup

    VLAN was created as a subinterface on the worker node NICs with assigned static IP addresses. The routing table output from a worker node confirms the VLAN interface and its associated subnets:

    # Sample routing table output
    [root@ocp-node-1 core] # ip r
    default via <gateway-ip> dev br-ex proto static
    <cluster-subnet> via <cluster-gateway> dev ovn-k8s-mp0
    <vlan-subnet> dev <nic>.<vlan-id> proto kernel scope link src <vlan-ip>

    This VLAN interface provides dedicated subnets for iSCSI traffic and enable independent connectivity path to storage systems.

    For more information, see the Dell Host Connectivity Guide for Linux.

iSCSI configuration

  • iSCSI on Worker nodes

    To enable iSCSI-based storage access, the Dell team activated the iscsi and iscsid services on all worker nodes. These services manage iSCSI session logins and maintain active connections with PowerStore targets.

    1. Start and validate the iscsi device: 
      systemctl start iscsi
      systemctl status iscsi
    2. Start and validate the iscsid service: 
      systemctl start iscsid
      systemctl status iscsid
    3. Enable both services to persist across reboots: 
      systemctl enable iscsi
      systemctl enable iscsid

    Once enabled, the worker nodes are prepared for iSCSI target discovery and login.

iSCSI configuration

  • iSCSI discovery setup

    Each worker node is configured with an iSCSI interface.

    1. Verify the initiator name: 
      cat /etc/iscsi/initiatorname.iscsi
    2. Create an iSCSI interface for VLAN 1078: 
      iscsiadm --m iface -I iface0 --o new
      iscsiadm --m iface -I iface0 -o update -n iface.net_ifacename -v <nic>.<vlan-id>
      1. Discover targets:
        iscsiadm -m discovery -t st -p <system-ip>:3260 -I iface0
      2. Log in to targets:
        iscsiadm -m node -T <target-iqn> -I iface0 -l
    3. Verify two active sessions: 
      iscsiadm -m session

iSCSI configuration

  • Multipath configuration

    To enhance storage resiliency and load balancing, it is recommended to implement device‑mapper multipathing on all worker nodes.

    1. Enable multipath: 
      mpathconf --enable --with_multipathd y
      systemctl restart multipathd
      systemctl enable --now multipathd
    2. Configure /etc/multipath.conf with PowerStore-specific settings: 
      defaults {
          user_friendly_names yes
      }

      devices {
          device {
              vendor "DellEMC"
              product "PowerStore"
              path_selector "queue-length 0"
              path_grouping_policy "group_by_prio"
              path_checker "tur"
              detect_prio yes
              failback immediate
              rr_min_io_rq 1
              hardware_handler "1 alua"
              prio "alua"
              fast_io_fail_tmo 15
              max_sectors_kb 1024
          }
      }
    3. Validate the configuration: 
      #cat /etc/multipath.conf

Logical architecture

  • The following diagram shows the logical architecture of this solution:

    In this solution, the figure illustrates a dual‑cluster RHOCP architecture engineered specifically for disaster recovery using PowerStore storage systems. Red Hat OpenShift Assisted Installer is used to deploy three bare‑metal, compute‑only nodes at each site, forming an independent RHOCP cluster per location. Each cluster consists of three control plane/worker nodes that host containerized applications and virtual machine workloads. These nodes run on RHCOS and use CRI‑O as the native container runtime.

    A dedicated replication link connects the two PowerStore storage systems, ensuring continuous data synchronization between source and destination volumes to support rapid recovery during site‑level outages. CSM Replication sidecar is deployed alongside the CSI driver on each RHOCP cluster, enabling dynamic persistent volume provisioning and orchestrating storage‑level replication for Kubernetes workloads. This ensures that application data remains consistent and recoverable across sites.

    Shared management services—including DNS, NTP, and a Bastion node—are centrally positioned in the architecture to provide common access for provisioning, automation, and platform operations. During failover events, these shared services help streamline cluster access, recovery operations, and workload redeployment across sites.

    Additional information

    • For more information about PowerStore host connectivity and storage systems, see Dell Technologies documentation.
    • For more information about the configuration of RHOCP cluster, see Red Hat documentation.

Home > Storage > PowerStore > White Papers > Building Resiliency for Red Hat OpenShift with Dell PowerStore and CSM Replication > Network architecture

Network architecture

  • The following diagram shows the network architecture of this solution:

    At the physical network layer, two supported Top‑of‑Rack (ToR) switches are deployed to ensure redundancy, traffic separation, and load balancing across the environment. In the network architecture, each PowerStore storage system maintains high‑availability connections to both ToR switches, ensuring continuous data access even during individual link or switch failures. A peer link between the ToR switches enables inter‑switch communication, multi‑pathing, and resilient traffic forwarding.

    In this failover‑ready architecture, each RHOCP compute host connects to the PowerStore systems using the iSCSI protocol. Dedicated iSCSI storage networks are configured on PowerStore to provide block‑level access to persistent volumes for both containerized and virtualized applications. PowerStore requires all configured networks to be unique; therefore, Dell Technologies strongly recommends deploying storage and replication networks on separate, unique VLANs to isolate traffic flows and enhance fault tolerance. This ensures efficient data transfer for CSM‑driven storage replication while preventing interference with application, management, or storage I/O traffic. In the event of a site failure, this network segmentation enables rapid and consistent data recovery, supporting seamless failover of Kubernetes persistent volumes and VM workloads to the secondary RHOCP cluster.

    For more information about storage service networking and configuration using the PowerStore Manager, see the Dell PowerStore T and Q Networking Guide for Storage Services.

    The RHOCP compute nodes first create a bonded interface by combining two physical network interfaces for redundancy and increased resilience. A bridge interface is then layered on top of this bonded interface to support additional network abstraction. Finally, VLAN interfaces are configured on the bridge, allowing different types of traffic to be logically segmented and isolated.

    The following table shows the different networks that are configured for this solution:

    Table 3. Network configuration details
    Network type VLAN-ID Description
    Replication Network 1073 PowerStore storage system - A ↔ PowerStore storage system - B
    iSCSI 1 1076 RHOCP Nodes → PowerStore storage system - A
    iSCSI 2 1078 RHOCP Nodes → PowerStore storage system - B
    Management Network 1079 PowerStore storage systems, RHOCP iDRACs, Bastion, DNS, NTP

Prerequisites

  • A single‑replica PostgreSQL pod is deployed using replication storage class to simplify failover testing and maintain predictable behavior during evaluation. The database runs on a certified PostgreSQL container image and is made available internally through a ClusterIP service, ensuring secure in‑cluster access over the standard PostgreSQL port.

    For information about configuring PostgreSQL, see PostgreSQL documentation.

    1. Verify the deployment of the stateful application on the RHOCP cluster at the primary site by checking the status of the application pods. 
      [root@ocp-csah postgresql]# oc get pods -n powerstore
      NAME                                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
      postgresql-0                             1/1     Running   0          15h
      powerstore-controller-74f444897b-kkt6k   6/6     Running   0          14d
      powerstore-controller-74f444897b-mv55h   6/6     Running   0          14d
      powerstore-node-j5c8f                    3/3     Running   0          14d
      powerstore-node-p52pn                    3/3     Running   0          14d
      powerstore-node-sbsgl                    3/3     Running   0          14d
    2. Verify that the PV and PVC are created on the source cluster. 
      [root@ocp-csah ocp1]# oc get pv
      NAME                CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS   CLAIM                                     STORAGECLASS             VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS   REASON   AGE
      csivol-c1f203a386   64Gi       RWO            Retain           Bound    powerstore/postgresql-data-postgresql-0   powerstore-replication   <unset>                          21m

      [root@ocp-csah ocp1]# oc get pvc
      NAME                           STATUS   VOLUME              CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS             VOLUMEATTRIBUTESCLASS   AGE
      postgresql-data-postgresql-0   Bound    csivol-c1f203a386   64Gi       RWO            powerstore-replication   <unset>                 21m
    3. Verify the status of the replication group.
    4. Verify the status of the volume group from PowerStore UI.
    5. Log in to the PostgreSQL database and insert some data to validate the failover operation. 
      # kubectl exec -it postgresql-0 -- bash
      Defaulted container "postgresql" out of: postgresql, fix-perms (init)
      bash-5.1$ psql -U admin -d mydb
      psql (16.10)
      Type "help" for help.

      mydb=> INSERT INTO users (username, email)
      VALUES
          ('alice', 'alice@example.com'),
          ('bob', 'bob@example.com'),
          ('charlie', 'charlie@example.com').
      INSERT 0 3

Prerequisites

  • To deploy OpenShift Virtualization, ensure that your OCP cluster runs version 4.6 or later (4.14 or newer is recommended) and includes at least three worker nodes. Each node must have CPU virtualization extensions enabled—vmx for Intel processors or svm for AMD—along with a minimum of 16 GB of RAM (32 GB or more is recommended for hosting multiple VMs) and at least two CPU cores. You can verify CPU virtualization support by running:

    lscpu | grep Virtualization

    Administrator permissions are required, and the oc CLI must be installed, configured, and authenticated with an admin-level account. The cluster must have a default StorageClass for provisioning VM disks, and a properly configured persistent storage backend such as the Dell PowerStore CSI driver.

Protecting Containerized Applications

  • This chapter describes the data protection and DR to target site by leveraging the native synchronous CSM Replication capabilities of the Dell PowerStore storage array. It provides automatic, policy-based replication of PVs so that stateful applications can failover and reprotect between clusters during planned or unplanned outages. Validation activities are conducted within a dedicated namespace in the RHOCP cluster. For instance, storage class is configured with synchronous replication to carry out the failover use cases on containerized workloads.

Setup and Protect Virtualized workloads

  • This section describes the procedure for deploying Virtualization on an OCP cluster. The deployment leverages the OpenShift Virtualization Operator and the HCO to enable VM workloads alongside containerized applications. The cluster needs to meet all virtualization prerequisites, including CPU virtualization support, adequate memory and CPU capacity, and a default StorageClass provided by the PowerStore CSI driver.

    The deployment process includes enabling OperatorHub sources, installing the OpenShift Virtualization Operator, creating the HyperConverged custom resource, and validating the installation. Once these steps are complete, you can begin creating and managing VMs using either the OpenShift Web Console or the CLI.

    This chapter also outlines data protection and disaster recovery for OpenShift Virtualization using Dell PowerStore’s native synchronous replication. In PowerStore synchronous replication, the destination (remote) copy of the data is kept in a fully synchronized, zero‑RPO state. To ensure data consistency, the destination resource is typically placed in a write‑protected (read‑only) state.

    It enables automatic, policy-driven replication of PVs allowing stateful VM workloads to failover between clusters during planned or unplanned outages. All validation is performed in a dedicated OpenShift namespace, where a synchronous‑replication StorageClass is used to test failover scenarios.

Use case 1: Planned Failover of Containerized Applications

  • Test procedure

    The PostgreSQL application running at the primary site is FailedOver to the target site.

    Follow the steps below to perform this activity:
    1. All I/O operations are currently occurring on the primary site.
    2. To initiate the planned failover, gracefully shut down the application running on the primary site. 
      # oc scale statefulset postgresql --replicas=0 -n powerstore
      statefulset.apps/postgresql scaled
       
      # oc get sts -n powerstore
      NAME         READY   AGE
      postgresql   0/0     86m
      Note: When users do Failover and Failback, the tests pods on the source cluster may go “CrashLoopOff” state since it will try to remount the same volume which is already mounted. To get around this problem, bring down the number of replicas to 0 and then after that is done, bring it up to 1.

    3. Verify the Replication group status. 
      # oc get dellcsireplicationgroup -n powerstore
      NAME                                      AGE    STATE   PG ID                                  LINK STATE     LAST LINKSTATE UPDATE
      rg-30dca403-0f4d-422e-93fd-3dc6fea2ae1f   115m   Ready   1be58e31-4c3d-458c-8f9f-ec8dadb9d1d5   SYNCHRONIZED   2025-12-11T08:41:15Z
    4. Initiate the planned failover operation by performing the repctl command. 
      # ./repctl --rg rg-30dca403-0f4d-422e-93fd-3dc6fea2ae1f failover --target ocp-2
      [2025-12-11 03:52:02]  INFO RG (rg-30dca403-0f4d-422e-93fd-3dc6fea2ae1f), successfully updated with action: failover
    5. Verify the updated status of the replication group.
    6. Verify the failover status in the PowerStore UI.

Use case 1: Planned Failover of Containerized Applications

  • Test results

    Once the failover occurs from the primary site to the target site, we can bring up the application at the target site with synchronized and replicated PV and PVC mapped to it. CSM does not start or stop applications, application startups is performed manually or automated depending on the user’s design.

    Follow the steps below to validate the failover at the target site:

    Note: CSM Replication does not replicate or manage application-level Kubernetes manifests—such as StatefulSets, Deployments, SecurityContext, or InitContainers—across clusters. Therefore, administrators must deploy these artifacts on the DR cluster and ensure file system ownership and permissions on replicated volumes are correct so applications can start successfully after failover.

    1. When bringing up the PostgreSQL pod at the target site, provide volume ownership/permissions so the container’s group can write. 
      spec:
            securityContext:
              runAsUser: 999
              runAsGroup: 999
              fsGroup: 999
      chown -R 999:999 /var/lib/postgresql/data
      chmod -R g+rwX /var/lib/postgresql/data
    2. Verify the PostgreSQL application deployment. 
      # oc get pods -n powerstore
      NAME                                     READY   STATUS    RESTARTS      AGE
      postgresql-0                             1/1     Running   0             14h
      powerstore-controller-864d889dd8-47g89   7/7     Running   3 (22h ago)   22h
      powerstore-controller-864d889dd8-5x7zk   7/7     Running   3 (22h ago)   22h
      powerstore-node-cpkvn                    3/3     Running   0             22h
      powerstore-node-xsvdd                    3/3     Running   0             22h
      powerstore-node-zdxvr                    3/3     Running   0             22h
    3. Verify the replicated data by logging into the PostgreSQL database. 
      # kubectl exec -it postgresql-0 -- bash
      Defaulted container "postgresql" out of: postgresql, fix-perms (init)
      bash-5.1$ psql -U admin -d mydb
      psql (16.10)
      Type "help" for help.
       
      mydb=> SELECT * FROM users;
       id | username |        email        |         created_at
      ----+----------+---------------------+----------------------------
        1 | alice    | alice@example.com   | 2025-12-11 07:07:04.355608
        2 | bob      | bob@example.com     | 2025-12-11 07:07:04.355608
        3 | charlie  | charlie@example.com | 2025-12-11 07:07:04.355608
      (3 rows)
    4. Write new data and verify that writes are enabled on the target site. 
      mydb=> INSERT INTO users (username, email)
      VALUES
          ('aby', 'aby@example.com'),
          ('john', 'john@example.com'),
          ('joe', '@example.com');
      INSERT 0 3
      mydb=> SELECT * FROM users;
       id | username |        email        |         created_at
      ----+----------+---------------------+----------------------------
        1 | alice    | alice@example.com   | 2025-12-11 07:07:04.355608
        2 | bob      | bob@example.com     | 2025-12-11 07:07:04.355608
        3 | charlie  | charlie@example.com | 2025-12-11 07:07:04.355608
        4 | aby      | aby@example.com     | 2025-12-12 06:25:03.496878
        5 | john     | john@example.com    | 2025-12-12 06:25:03.496878
        6 | joe      | @example.com        | 2025-12-12 06:25:03.496878
      (6 rows)

Use case 1: Planned Failover of Virtualized workloads

  • Test procedure

    Verify operations

    Verify the status of the below operations before initiating failover.

    1. I/O operations are currently occurring on the primary site.
    2. The source volume group is shown with a synchronous replication protection policy applied.
    3. Replication group status shows both source and target are synchronized.

    Perform failover operation

    Follow the steps below to perform failover operation:
    1. Make sure VM is in turned off state or volumes are not in locked state.
    2. Perform the failover command: 
      [root@ocp-csah repctl]# ./repctl --rg rg-221c5c3e-d134-4609-938e-4f321c03f43d failover --target ocp-2
      [2026-01-07 02:55:21]  INFO RG (rg-221c5c3e-d134-4609-938e-4f321c03f43d), successfully updated with action: failover
    3. Verify that the Replication Group Status shows failedover state. 
      [root@ocp-csah repctl]# ./repctl get rg
      [2026-01-07 02:56:04]  INFO listing replication groups
      [2026-01-07 02:56:04]  INFO Cluster: ocp-1
      +-----+
      | RG  |
      +-----+
      Name                                    State   rClusterID      Driver                          RemoteRG                                IsSource        LinkState
      rg-221c5c3e-d134-4609-938e-4f321c03f43d Ready   ocp-2           csi-powerstore.dellemc.com      rg-221c5c3e-d134-4609-938e-4f321c03f43d false           FAILEDOVER
      [2026-01-07 02:56:04]  INFO
      [2026-01-07 02:56:04]  INFO Cluster: ocp-2
      +-----+
      | RG  |
      +-----+
      Name                                    State   rClusterID      Driver                          RemoteRG                                IsSource        LinkState
      rg-221c5c3e-d134-4609-938e-4f321c03f43d Ready   ocp-1           csi-powerstore.dellemc.com      rg-221c5c3e-d134-4609-938e-4f321c03f43d true            FAILEDOVER
      [2026-01-07 02:56:04]  INFO
    4. Verify failover status from the PowerStore UI.

Use case 1: Planned Failover of Virtualized workloads

  • Test results

    After the planned failover from the primary site to the target site, the virtual machines can be brought online at the target cluster using their fully synchronized and replicated PVs and PVCs. This ensures that the VM workloads resume with consistent storage state and minimal disruption.

    Follow the steps below to validate the failover:

    1. Check the replicated volumes status at the target site.
    2. Attach these replicated volumes to the target VM and login to the PostgreSQL database to verify the replicated data.

Use case 2: Reprotect from new source

  • Objective

    After failover, a re‑protect operation reverses the replication flow so the target cluster—now running the active VMs—replicates data back to the original site. This restores continuous data protection and prepares the environment for future failback.

Use case 2: Reprotect to Resume Replication

  • Objective

    The objective of this use case is to restore disaster‑recovery readiness after a failover, reprotection reverses the replication flow so the new primary site begins replicating data back to the original (or alternate) site. This enables future failback, and maintains business continuity.

Use case 3: Unplanned Failover of Containerized Applications

  • Objective

    The objective of this use case is to ensure that during an unplanned outage at the primary site, the PostgreSQL application and its associated workloads automatically fail over to the target site and are successfully recovered with full write access, ensuring continuous data availability and minimal service disruption.

Use case 3: Unplanned Failover of Containerized Applications

  • Test procedure

    To simulate an unplanned failover scenario in the lab environment, we performed the following steps:

    1. Pause the replication between the primary and target sites.
    2. Simulate a primary site outage by powering off all primary site nodes, thereby making the entire primary site unavailable.
    3. Initiated the unplanned failover at the target site using repctl command. 
      # ./repctl –rg  rg-407192ce-eed7-474d-b786-614dbfc42c99 failover –target ocp-2 --unplanned

Virtual Machine setup

  • Install Virtual Machine

    To deploy a VM in OpenShift Virtualization, start by choosing a bootable volume.

    Choose an instance type that matches the workload requirements, such as general-purpose or memory-intensive configurations.

    Configure the VM by specifying its name, operating system, CPU and memory allocation, disk size, and storage class. Assign the VM to a project namespace and, optionally, configure SSH access.

    Verify that the virtual machine is created.

Virtual Machine setup

  • Persistent Volume Claim creation

    Create two Data Volumes and attach them to the VM for application use.

    1. Log in to the Red Hat OpenShift console.
    2. Go to Storage > PersistentVolumeClaims.
    3. Click Create PersistentVolumeClaims > With Form.
    4. Select the storage class, access mode, size, volume mode and click Create.
    5. Verify PVC and its corresponding PV are created automatically.
    6. We can now map these PVCs to VM.
      1. Go to VM > Configuration > Storage.
      2. Click Add disk > Volume.
      3. Click Save.
    7. View the mapped volumes inside the VM.
    8. Power on the VM and verify the mounted volumes.

Virtualization Operator deployment

  • Enable OperatorHub source

    Ensure that the Red Hat operators are visible:

    #oc get operatorhub.config.openshift.io/cluster -o yaml
    #oc patch operatorhub.config.openshift.io/cluster --type merge \
      -p '{"spec":{"disableAllDefaultSources":false}}'
